title: How many? — numbers and classifiers
goal: Count things with classifiers — the counting words you half-know from "a loaf of", "a sheet of", "two head of" — and master the three number exceptions you must memorize.
bekal: count with the pattern **number + classifier + noun**, like "three volumes (of) book"
say numbers up to a thousand, including *mười lăm*, *hai mươi mốt* and *hai mươi lăm*

notes: **Classifiers aren't as strange as they look.** English says "a **loaf** of bread", "a **sheet** of paper", "two **head** of cattle". Vietnamese does the same thing, with the pattern **number + classifier + noun** — but for every noun you count, and with no "of". One difference matters: in Vietnamese the classifier is **required**. *Hai sách* is wrong; *hai quyển sách* is right.

**Cái is the all-purpose classifier.** If you forget the right classifier for an object, use *cái* — you'll be understood and won't sound rude. Living, moving creatures take *con*, people take *người*. Those three already cover most A1 conversation.

**Classifiers are also used WITHOUT a number**, to point at one particular thing: *cái bàn này* (this table), *con mèo kia* (that cat over there). Here the classifier works a bit like "the": it turns a general noun into the specific thing being talked about.

**Mấy and bao nhiêu both mean "how many".** *Mấy* is used when you expect a **small** answer (under ten): *mấy người bạn?*, *mấy giờ?* *Bao nhiêu* is used when the answer could be large or is completely unknown: *bao nhiêu tiền?*, *bao nhiêu tuổi?* Using the wrong one isn't fatal, but it sounds foreign.

**Nữa means "more, again" and goes at the end; thêm means "add" and goes before the verb.** They often appear together: *mua thêm một quyển nữa* = "buy one more". For ordering food, this is the pair to memorize: *cho tôi một ly nữa* = "another glass, please".

**Cho tôi … is literally "give me …", and that's how you order.** It isn't a rude command: in Vietnamese it's the most natural way to ask for anything in a shop, stall or café. Adding *ạ* at the end makes it polite: *Cho tôi hai cái ạ.*

grammars.title: Numbers — and three exceptions to memorize
body: Vietnamese numbers are beautifully regular up to ten, then hide three traps in the tens. None of them makes sense, none follows a rule, and they simply have to be memorized.
after: ⚠️ **The three exceptions:** (1) **10** becomes *mươi* inside multiples of ten — *hai mươi*, not *hai mười*; (2) **5** becomes *lăm* after tens — *mười lăm*, *hai mươi lăm*; (3) **1** becomes *mốt* after tens other than *mười* — *hai mươi mốt*, but still *mười một* for 11.

The number **4** has two forms: *bốn* for counting, *tư* in sequences and dates — *thứ tư* (Wednesday, literally "fourth in order"), *mùng bốn* (the 4th). At A1 just use *bốn*, and recognize *tư* when you read it.

grammars.title: Classifiers: the ten that cover A1
body: Vietnamese has dozens of classifiers, but the ten below are enough for all everyday conversation. The rest you can replace with *cái* without sounding wrong.

head: Classifier
For
English feel
Example
rows: animals; also rivers, knives, roads, numbers
vehicles, one of a pair, stylish objects
*một bát phở* — a bowl of phở
*một đôi giày* — a pair of shoes

after: ⚠️ Some classifiers differ between north and south: the north uses *quyển*, *bát*, *quả*, *cốc*; the south uses *cuốn*, *tô*, *trái*, *ly*. Both are understood everywhere. This course uses the northern forms, but mentions the southern partners because you're sure to hear them.

**Con is used for some inanimate things that "move or stretch out"**: *con sông* (river), *con đường* (road), *con dao* (knife), *con số* (number). There's no rule you could guess; learn them as small exceptions, and use *cái* if you forget.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Asking an adult's age with *mấy tuổi* sounds like you're talking to a kindergartner. With adults it's always *bao nhiêu tuổi*, and with someone much older, softer still: *Bác năm nay bao nhiêu tuổi ạ?*

blocks.title: Why age comes up so fast
items: You saw the reason in Unit 1: Vietnamese pronouns are chosen by age, so the other person **can't build a sentence** until they know whether you're older or younger. An age question in the first few minutes isn't nosiness — it's a grammatical need.

Vietnamese people also often place age by birth year in the zodiac rather than by number: *Anh tuổi con gì?* = "What's your zodiac animal?". An answer like *Tuổi Ngựa* (Year of the Horse) is enough — a tactful way to give your age without saying the number.

blocks.text: The last row shows the full order of a Vietnamese noun phrase, and it never changes: **classifier → noun → adjective → pointer**. English runs the other way ("this new table"); Vietnamese says "item table new this".

⚠️ If there's a number, it goes first and the pointer still goes last: *hai cái bàn mới này* = "these two new tables". No part ever moves, in any sentence. Vietnamese is extremely faithful to its order, and that's exactly what makes it easy to learn.
